tldr: By persistently maintaining geometric and contact constraint programs generated from natural language—from MPC simulation verification all the way through reinforcement learning and data generation—this research achieves robust zero-shot real-robot execution without dense manual rewards or human demonstrations.
hero_caption: Overview of the entire Kuafu lifecycle. Typed SUN Programs are generated from language instructions, pre-verified with MPC in physical simulation, and then consistently retained as behavior anchors for BC, rewards for residual RL, and monitors for data production.
overview:
When learning long-horizon, multi-stage robot manipulation, reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful tool capable of acquiring rich contact-rich behaviors. However, hand-engineering dense rewards for each stage requires tremendous effort. While recent methods prompt LLMs to write reward functions, verifying each candidate reward requires running a heavy RL training loop, which makes iteration extremely time-consuming. On the other hand, optimization-based methods such as Model Predictive Control (MPC) can explicitly model task geometry, but they are vulnerable to modeling errors and lack robustness on real robots.

This research asks: can we bridge MPC's fast verification capability with RL's robust execution ability? In conventional pipelines, the moment MPC generates trajectories, the underlying constraints and stage transition semantics—explaining *why* those actions were correct—are discarded. This leads to semantic drift in downstream learning, where the policy diverges from the original task intent.

To solve this, the authors introduce "SUN Programs," a typed, executable task representation. Grounded relations and satisfaction criteria generated from language instructions are compiled at once into MPC costs, stage transition conditions, and RL rewards, and the exact same program is retained across the entire pipeline. Invalid instructions are immediately rejected at the low-cost MPC stage, and only verified structures are carried over into residual RL and high-quality data production.

Evaluated on nine challenging tasks in Isaac Lab, Kuafu achieves an 82.03% macro success rate, vastly outperforming sparse-reward baselines (35.67%) and pure imitation learning (24.75%). Furthermore, visual policies trained on the generated data achieve a 34.7% zero-shot success rate on real Franka and Kinova robots without any additional real-world fine-tuning.
contributions: Proposed "SUN Programs," typed executables that unify task semantics across control (MPC), monitoring, and reinforcement learning (Residual RL) to prevent semantic drift.

Built "Kuafu," an end-to-end system that automatically synthesizes SUN Programs from language instructions, pre-screens their physical feasibility via simulation MPC, and amortizes them into policies.

Achieved an 82.03% success rate across nine long-horizon manipulation tasks without dense manual rewards or human seed demonstrations, at roughly one-fourth the compute cost of prior LLM reward search methods (Eureka).
Demonstrated zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on two physical robot platforms (Franka and Kinova) using vision-based policies (such as DP3) trained on the autonomously generated data.

sections.heading: Persistent programs that resolve the disconnect between control and learning
sections.summary: RL handles contact-rich dynamics well but struggles with reward engineering, while MPC explicitly models structure but is sensitive to model errors. This work proposes persistent "SUN Programs" to prevent task structure from being lost across the handoff between the two paradigms.
sections.details:
For multi-stage robot manipulation, reinforcement learning (RL) is an appealing approach that directly acquires high-dimensional, contact-rich behaviors. However, manually engineering and tuning intermediate "dense rewards" is notoriously labor-intensive. While recent works prompt large language models (LLMs) to write reward code, verifying whether a candidate reward works requires training a full policy from scratch each time, creating a severe latency bottleneck in the iteration loop.

Conversely, model-based planning methods like Model Predictive Control (MPC) explicitly formulate geometric goals and transition conditions, making them well-suited for testing and repairing behaviors under closed-loop dynamics. Yet, they remain extremely fragile against modeling errors and observation noise, lacking real-world robustness.

A common way to combine them is to generate successful trajectories with MPC and distill them via imitation learning (Behavior Cloning: BC). However, this introduces an overlooked disconnect: passing only numeric trajectories discards the entire semantic intent of the task—such as constraints and stage-completion predicates explaining *why* those actions were correct. Consequently, downstream policy learning requires defining separate rewards, leading to "semantic drift" where learning behavior diverges from verified control intent.

To address this, the authors argue for "persistent task programs" that survive closed-loop testing in physical simulation. This is embodied in "Semantically UNified (SUN) Programs" and the orchestrating system "Kuafu." Crucially, optimization (MPC) is repurposed not merely as a trajectory generator, but as a fast screener of task knowledge.

sections.heading: The lineage of executable programs and hybrid control-learning methods
sections.summary: This section surveys symbolic planning, LLM reward generation, and control-to-policy distillation for long-horizon manipulation. Kuafu stands apart by persisting task representations across the entire pipeline rather than restricting them to a single phase.
sections.details:
Related work spans three primary areas:

- Executable task representations: Symbolic planning and program generation have long sought to bridge discrete steps with continuous motions. Recent methods like ReKep optimize 3D keypoint cost functions, while OmniManip combines 3D spatial constraints with VLMs. However, these formulations remain confined to a single planning or control phase and are not retained through the policy learning stage.
- Control-to-policy transfer: Methods like Eureka and Text2Reward use LLMs to write executable reward code, but they suffer from the high computational cost of full RL training for every revision. Approaches such as LATO and MPC-Net distill MPC policies, and Residual RL augments nominal controllers with learned residuals, yet they typically require re-implementing stage predicates and task structures from scratch.
- Autonomous robot data generation: Frameworks like MimicGen and SkillMimic augment a few human demonstrations via spatial transformations to produce large-scale imitation data. However, they remain bounded by the original demonstrations and lack independent mechanisms to monitor and verify learned policy rollouts.

Kuafu integrates these threads: relational definitions and termination predicates remain consistent throughout MPC pre-verification, policy acquisition, residual learning, and data production monitoring.

sections.heading: Inside Kuafu: From synthesis and verification to residual learning and data production
sections.summary: An LLM constructs a SUN Program using a typed operator library, and MPC immediately verifies its physical feasibility. Successful trajectories anchor a Stage-BC policy, which bounded residual RL refines before scaling up data production.
sections.details:
Kuafu's pipeline consists of four main stages:

### III-A Semantically UNified (SUN) Programs
At the core lies the "SUN Program $\Gamma$." Rather than letting an LLM write unconstrained code, it composes programs by binding registered coordinate frames $\mathcal{F}$ (e.g., object grasp sites, drawer sliding axes) to a typed operator library $\mathcal{L}$ (`align_axis`, `direction_move`, `fix_orientation`, etc.). This structure prevents LLM hallucinations. Defined relations are automatically and simultaneously compiled into MPC cost terms $\phi^{\mathrm{mpc}}$, stage satisfaction predicates $P$, and RL cost terms $c^{\mathrm{rl}}$—a process termed "Semantic Unification."

### III-B Program Validation and Acceptance
Instead of launching RL immediately, Kuafu screens the candidate program's physical feasibility by executing MPC in simulation. Testing across 10 initial conditions, a program is accepted only if it satisfies an external oracle $g_{\text{ext}}$ without internal predicate inconsistencies (avoiding false completions). Failed programs undergo up to 5 rounds of automated repair. This MPC-level filtering eliminates wasted RL training runs.

### III-C SUN-Guided Policy Amortization
Using the accepted SUN Program and 1,000 successful MPC trajectories, Kuafu amortizes control into a policy. First, a stage-conditioned behavior cloning policy (Stage-BC) $\pi_{\theta}$ is trained on MPC demonstrations and frozen as a behavioral anchor. Next, a bounded residual policy $\pi_{\psi}$ is trained via PPO to provide fine-grained corrections. Rewards are automatically computed from normalized stage progress scores $S_k$ to enforce monotonic advancement. An LLM agent monitors training curves to calibrate reward weights and the residual bound $\rho_{\max}$.

### III-D Data Production
The trained policy executes rollouts to mass-produce demonstrations for downstream vision policies (models operating directly from camera images). During rollout, the SUN Program monitor acts as a sentinel to filter out falsely completed trajectories. The resulting dataset strips all privileged state information and program traces, outputting clean observation-action pairs for downstream training.

sections.heading: Evaluated on nine challenging tasks: Superior success rates and compute efficiency
sections.summary: Kuafu achieved an 82.03% success rate across nine long-horizon, multi-stage manipulation tasks in Isaac Lab. It trained roughly 4x faster than Eureka, and DP3 policies trained on its data achieved a 34.7% zero-shot success rate on real hardware.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted in Isaac Lab across 8,192 parallel simulation environments on nine tasks: emergency stop button press and twist (T0, T3), block stacking (T1: 2 blocks, T6: 3 blocks), drawer manipulation (T2: open, T7: open and place), bottle uprighting (T4), pen insertion (T5), and mug hanging (T8).

### IV-A Formulation Reliability
Across 45 independent runs, 29 passed on the first attempt, and 14 of the remaining 16 passed after diagnostic-guided auto-repair, achieving a 95.6% final acceptance rate. Average LLM token consumption was 110.5k tokens per task, far lower than Eureka (234.4k tokens) or VoxPoser (which invokes LLMs per execution step).

### IV-B Performance and Ablation Analysis
Kuafu achieved an 82.03% macro success rate across all tasks. By contrast, ablations using the Stage-BC anchor with sparse-reward RL reached 35.67%, and standalone Stage-BC reached 24.75%. Pure RL without anchors and unconstrained residual variants collapsed to 0% across all tasks. Eureka suffered from overfitting (12.85%), while online-optimized VoxPoser lagged at 10.00%.
Kuafu showed remarkable resilience to task horizon. Extending block stacking from 8 stages (T1) to 15 stages (T6) dropped success from 95.78% to 87.25%—a modest 8.53 percentage point decrease. While baseline methods dropped to near 0% on long-horizon tasks T6 and T7, Kuafu maintained strong performance. In compute cost, Kuafu required 122.67 GPU hours versus Eureka's 479.60 GPU hours, proving roughly 3.91x more computationally efficient.

### IV-C Data Efficiency
To assess data quality, 500 trajectories per task were used to train a fixed 3D diffusion policy (DP3). The DP3 policy trained on Kuafu's data attained a 46.02% success rate, more than double the strongest alternative, SkillMimic (22.44%). Data throughput reached 246.79 minutes of successful trajectories per GPU hour, which is 10.57x faster than human teleoperation (23.34 min/hour).

### IV-D Visual Learning and Zero-Shot Transfer
Collecting 1,000 simulation trajectories, physical experiments were conducted on Franka and Kinova robot platforms. In zero-shot transfer without any real-world fine-tuning, Kuafu achieved a 34.72% macro success rate across 106 trials in 6 tasks (36/106 overall, 33.96% pooled). The primary failure mode was millimeter-level grasping inaccuracies (e.g., T1 success was 15%), whereas basic geometric alignment and stage transitions transferred reliably to physical hardware.

sections.heading: Preserving semantics is the shortest path to smart and robust policies
sections.summary: This section summarizes Kuafu's effectiveness in maintaining MPC-verified typed programs through learning and data collection, while discussing its underlying assumptions, challenges, and limitations.
sections.details:
This work presented "SUN Programs" as an enduring bridge between control and learning, along with its harness system "Kuafu." Task semantics validated during model-based control deliver their true value when maintained persistently after policy learning, rather than being discarded as ephemeral trajectory traces. This enables efficient acquisition of robust, long-horizon, multi-stage manipulation skills without manual dense rewards or human demonstrations.

At the same time, the approach operates within defined scopes and limitations:
- Dependency on predefined interfaces: It relies on correctly registered object coordinate frames and axes, as well as a finite typed operator library. Deformable objects or fluids requiring new operator primitives cannot be handled out-of-the-box.
- Unverified open-world generalization: Generalization to unseen language instructions or novel operator primitives remains outside the scope of this study.
- Irreversible stage transitions: The stage monitor is strictly monotonic; it does not support automatic rollback or retry when physical failures occur (such as an object slipping from the gripper).
- Sim-to-real transfer precision: While zero-shot real-world transfer was demonstrated, grasping precision limits mean it does not yet guarantee flawless execution in unstructured environments.

takeaways: When transferring MPC solutions to learning pipelines, retaining task constraints and stage semantics alongside trajectory data is crucial to preventing long-horizon task collapse.
Restricting the LLM to typed operator library bindings and pre-screening with fast MPC simulations dramatically cuts wasteful RL training runs (reducing compute by ~4x).
Combining a Stage-BC behavioral anchor with bounded residual RL minimizes performance degradation even as the number of task stages increases.
Data produced under simulation program monitors is of high quality, enabling over 30% zero-shot real-robot transfer without real-world fine-tuning.
limitations: Requires pre-registered semantic assets such as local object coordinate frames and interaction axes; extending to completely novel objects or non-rigid items (cloth, fluids) requires new operator definitions.
Stage progression is strictly monotonic, lacking a rollback or retry mechanism to recover if an object slips or shifts mid-execution.
Real-world zero-shot success is limited to 34.7%, with sim-to-real gaps being especially noticeable during grasping phases that require millimeter-level precision.
